In Tagu et al. (2022, *Cognition*), people used a mouse to forage for
targets of three colours among distractors (54 items per trial) in two
conditions: a **value** condition, where one target colour was worth more
than the others, and a **control** condition without values. The question
is how value, proximity and priming (the type just selected) shape which
target is selected next.

Here the three target colours are the item classes of a categorical
(`cat`) model. In each block, class 1 is the block's designated colour
(the high-value colour in the value condition, a nominal category in the
control) and classes 2 and 3 are the other two colours, in colour-number
order, which is arbitrary: so only class 1 is comparable across people and
conditions.

*Note*: this is the only dataset here with more than two item classes,
so the only one that can test whether the full class-transition matrix
(`b_v`) is needed. With two classes the matrix is the same model as the
papers' class weight and stick/switch rate (`b_a`, `b_s`; see the
simulated cat example); with three it has six free probabilities against
their three (two class weights, one stick/switch rate).

This page shows how to work with a fitted model: checking convergence,
reading the posterior, accuracy and posterior predictive checks. It ends with a model comparison, three item classes against two.
The model is the default one: multi-level, Fourier-124 directions, the
default priors, 4 chains of 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling iterations.

*Note*: this page doesn't fit anything. It reads saved fits
(`tagu2022cog_fourier124.rds` and `tagu2022cog2items_fourier124.rds`) from `fits/` in this folder.
They aren't in the repository: to make them, run `fit_tagu2022cog.R` in this
folder (about 2.5 hours on a laptop), which saves them there. See
`examples/real_data/README.md`.

Code: `tagu2022cog.R`.

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::read_chunk("tagu2022cog.R")
```

## The fit

```{r read-fit}
```

Population-level estimates (medians and 97% HPDIs) and convergence.
R-hat and ESS are coloured green (good), orange (acceptable) or red
(bad). At 1000 iterations this fit's smallest bulk ESS is about 285:
fine for medians and intervals, but a published analysis might use 2000.

```{r fit-summary}
#| results: asis
```

Rank plots of the five worst-mixing parameters. If the chains have mixed
well, each chain's histogram is roughly flat and they overlap.


## Accuracy

The fit doesn't store a prediction for every selection
(`save_selections = FALSE`, the default), so `predict_fomo()` makes them
from 200 posterior draws. Deterministic accuracy is how often the item the
model judges most likely is the one selected; the probability of the
chosen item credits being nearly right too. Chance (dotted) is
1 / items left; the nearest-neighbour rule (dashed) always picks the
closest item, so the gap above it is what the model adds to proximity
alone. This is in-sample accuracy, which overestimates out-of-sample
accuracy.

```{r predict}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(file.mtime("fits/tagu2022cog_fourier124.rds"), rlang::hash(d))
```

```{r fig-accuracy}
#| fig-cap: "Accuracy at each selection, with chance and nearest-neighbour baselines."
```

## Posterior predictive check

Whole trials simulated from the fitted model, compared with the data. The
model doesn't predict when a trial stops, so each simulated trial keeps as
many selections as the observed one.

```{r sim-posterior}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(file.mtime("fits/tagu2022cog_fourier124.rds"), rlang::hash(d), n_post_draws)
```

```{r fig-sim-trial}
#| fig-cap: "One trial per condition, simulated from the fitted model."
```

```{r fig-sim-stats}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr rlang::hash(list(found_post, trial_stats))
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Trial statistics for the data (x) and simulated from the posterior (y). Points near the diagonal mean the model reproduces them."
```

## Model comparison: three item classes or two?

The fit above gives each target colour its own class, so the class
transitions are a 3 x 3 matrix. The simpler alternative merges the two
non-designated colours into one class (`tagu2022cog2items`: high-value
against the rest), leaving a 2 x 2 matrix. The selections are the same,
only the class labels differ, so the models' leave-one-out predictions of
each trial can be compared directly (the chunk checks that the two
datasets are identical apart from the class). The 2-class fit has the same
settings and is made by `fit_tagu2022cog.R` too.

```{r compare-load}
```

`fomo_compare()` tabulates accuracy (against the nearest-neighbour rule)
and loo. `elpd_diff` is the difference from the best model, `se_diff` its
standard error, and `robust` whether the difference survives dropping the
trials with unreliable (high Pareto k) loo estimates.

```{r compare}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(file.mtime("fits/tagu2022cog_fourier124.rds"), file.mtime("fits/tagu2022cog2items_fourier124.rds"), rlang::hash(d))
```

Three classes are far better: about 1,680 elpd ahead (SE 118), in both
conditions (below). Merging the two lower-value colours hides how people
move between them: in the 3-class fit, after selecting a colour-2 target
the next is more likely colour 2 than colour 3 (log-odds 1.1 in the value
condition, 1.5 in the control), and after colour 3 more likely colour 3
than colour 2 (1.4 in both). So people stick with the exact colour, not
just with "not the high-value colour", and they do so in the control
condition too, where no colour is worth more: this is priming by colour,
not value. About 9% of the 3-class model's trials have unreliable loo
estimates (high Pareto k), more than in the other datasets, but the
difference survives without those trials (`robust`). Three classes also
predict the next target better (accuracy 0.62 against 0.59).

```{r fig-compare}
#| fig-cap: "Difference in loo between the 3-class and 2-class models, summed over trials, by condition (point: sum; bars: 2 SE)."
```

For reference, the 2-class model's class transitions:

```{r fig-compare-cat}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(file.mtime("fits/tagu2022cog2items_fourier124.rds"), rlang::hash(d))
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "Per-person class-transition probabilities in the 2-class model."
```
